_readme: Hand-maintained HALF of the progress board — only what no API can know. Never hand-edit: use `node scripts/progress-board.mjs --start=<id> | --done=<id> | --block=<id> --why=… | --note=<id> --text=… | --add=… | --decide=<id> | --url=…`. Pull-request state is NOT stored here; it is derived live from `gh pr list` on every render.
_decisions: ENFORCED, not requested — the script refuses to render a board whose `awaiting` decisions cannot be answered from the page. Every one must carry `question`, at least two real `options` with exactly one `recommended`, and `ifNothing`; a missing field exits 1 naming the id and the field. `why` and `evidence` are strongly encouraged, not blocking. Build one with `--decision-add="<title>" --question=… --if-nothing=…` (lands as `draft`), then `--decision-option=<id> --label=… --detail=… [--recommend]`, `--decision-evidence=<id> --text=…`, `--decision-set=<id> --field=<title|question|why|ifNothing|detail|status|preparedDate> --value=…`, and finally `--decision-set=<id> --field=status --value=awaiting`. status: draft (being prepared, kept out of "needs you") | awaiting (outstanding, and therefore complete) | queued (RULED but deferred — its own section, never counted as needing you) | taken (absorbed into the plan, leaves the board).
_rulings: `ruling` (R1, R2, …) is the handle the operator quotes in chat — "R6 — as recommended". Assigned once from `nextRuling`, persisted, NEVER renumbered and NEVER reused: a taken or dropped decision retires its number with it. Every verb accepts either handle, so `--decide=R6` and `--decide=2978` reach the same decision. Do not hand-edit `ruling` or `nextRuling`.
_artifactUrl: Set once, with --url=<url>, right after the FIRST Artifact publish. Every later publish from a different session MUST pass this as the Artifact `url` parameter or a new URL is minted and the operator's bookmark dies.

decisions.title: Rule how a learning is admitted to agent memory — verify the note, rank by recurrence, block on nobody
decisions.question: Does a note reach agent memory on verified grounding, with recurrence demoted to ranking?
decisions.why: #1068 moved judgment from the close to the harvest for three sound reasons, but the close's faithfulness filter — quote the grounding turn or be rejected — was silently replaced by a recurrence count, on the assumption the transcript was gone. It is not gone. Whether that filter is restored, and what recurrence is for instead, is a judgment call the item frames as four linked forks to ratify together or reject one of.

options.label: Ratify all four defaults as one design
options.detail: verified grounding admits (1a), recurrence ranks only (2a), the pool entry carries the quoted turn (3a), a cadence fires the harvest (4a) — 1(a) is what makes 2(a) safe and 3(a) is what makes 1(a) cheap; it shrinks #1068 rather than repairing it

options.label: Keep the recurrence threshold as the admission gate
options.detail: #1068 as built; but it authenticates nothing, and it structurally excludes the one-off user directive, which is how essentially the whole existing corpus was created

options.label: Add a human approval step
options.detail: the safest-sounding option, and the one the operator has refused three times — it reverses a ratified non-blocking directive whose own grounding case was this exact pipeline

decisions.ifNothing: #1068 stays as built: admission rests on a forgeable count, the faithfulness filter it replaced stays lost, and the branch keeps drifting (29 commits behind main).
evidence: 4,481 session transcripts exist; 4,477 modified in the last 30 days — faithfulness was never structurally impossible
`session` and `ts` are emitter-written — four hand-written lines manufacture '2 sessions across 2 days' in one second
the 240/60/400 pool-entry cap is justified by exactly one thing: the #2610 channel, which does not exist

decisions.title: Converge loop — editor-enablement default by care band
decisions.question: At which care bands may the converge loop push fixes, rather than only report them?
decisions.why: The panel's rigor already scales by care band; the editor's enablement scales with nothing — it runs at every band, unexamined. A pass either mutates the author's branch or it does not, and that mutation is not reversible from the author's side, so this is a correctness and accountability call rather than a cost one.

options.label: Editor on below a care threshold, review-only at and above it
options.detail: bind enablement to the same careLevel that already dials the panel, inverted — editor at `low`, review-only at `elevated` and `high`; excludes the band where it was observed to fail and keeps leverage where fixes are mechanical. Ratify the threshold with it

options.label: Editor always on
options.detail: the built behaviour, and maximum leverage when it converges; on the one run we have it converged nothing and handed the human a branch mutated with a defect the original diff did not contain

options.label: Review-only everywhere
options.detail: safe and cheap, but it leaves the operator hand-fixing every finding, which is the problem the loop exists to solve

decisions.ifNothing: The loop stays editor-on at every band, and the answer gets discovered on other people's branches once it runs over a queue of parked PRs.
evidence: PR #1018 (`care: elevated`): the editor pushed a 15-file fix `729a9d8b`; round 2 faulted that repair three ways, incl. a fail-open in the gate the fix had just written
that run escalated having cleared nothing — 16 agents, 1.08M tokens, 56 minutes; the same disposition review-only would have reached
published: 45.1% of autonomously generated PRs require post-review fixes
`panelRigorForCareLevel` in `we:scripts/lib/jury-core.mjs` already dials by band; the editor does not

decisions.title: Define a "feature" tier above epic — deterministic feature to epic to slice rollup
decisions.question: How is a "feature" defined, so the feature to epic to slice rollup is deterministic?
decisions.why: The ratified feature-tracking screen (#2705) rolls up slice to epic to feature, but the backlog has no tier above epic. The `parent` chain alone cannot say which ancestor is the feature — it is deep and its roots are uneven — so determinism needs an explicitly-marked node, not a walk. The second half, whether that tier is enforced or merely nominal, is a genuine fork: both branches stay deterministic but yield permanently different trees.

options.label: An explicit `kind: feature` node, and a feature is a root (Fork 1b + Fork 2a)
options.detail: the only mechanism that is deterministic AND single-axis AND matches every surveyed tracker. Honest cost: epic-parity plumbing at six kind-keyed loader/gate sites, and promoting an epic like #2505 deletes its `parent: 2445` edge

options.label: An explicit `kind: feature` node, but leave its parent unconstrained (Fork 1b + Fork 2b)
options.detail: no migration and still deterministic, but the board then renders an epic structurally above features — the exact inversion the tier exists to remove. Take this if edge fidelity now beats board legibility

options.label: Derive the feature from `parent` chains (Fork 1a)
options.detail: no new field, but non-deterministic on the real tree: #2445 folds into one 87-item mega-feature and #2505/#2527 stop separating

options.label: A separate grouping field on epics, e.g. `feature: <NNN>` (Fork 1c)
options.detail: reintroduces the second structural axis #466 retired, kept in sync by hand and redundant with `parent`

decisions.ifNothing: The ratified feature-tracking screen (#2705) has no deterministic rollup to read, and #2733 stays blocked behind it.
evidence: measured over 2717 items / 205 epics: 81 of 88 epic parents are themselves epics; max parent-chain depth 5
#2445 has 87 descendants; #2505 and #2527 are separate rows in the ratified mock yet both carry `parent: 2445`
`BACKLOG_KINDS` at `we:scripts/check-standards-rules.mjs:40`; the tier deriver at `we:src/_data/backlog.js:186`
prior art: the tier above epic is an explicitly-marked node in Jira, Linear, Shortcut, Azure DevOps, GitHub and Asana — never a graph walk
governed by #466 (one structural `kind` axis); Fork 1b extends that axis rather than adding a second

decisions.title: Review independence vs the working pattern
decisions.question: Once the self-approval check lands, how do reviews get cleared?
decisions.ifNothing: #1100 cannot land, and #1098's narrowing rests on convention rather than a check.
decisions.why: Subagents inherit the parent session's CLAUDE_CODE_SESSION_ID. PRs are opened by subagents and verdicts recorded from the same session, so author and clearer are the same id. PR #1100 refuses that as a self-clear — correctly. It means the current pattern of "subagent reviews, main session records the accept" stops working.

options.label: Run reviews from a separate session
options.detail: makes the independence real rather than nominal; costs a second session per review round

options.label: The operator clears everything
options.detail: simple, but routes all verdicts back to a human, which is the opposite of the direction we are heading

options.label: Sanction and document the `env -u CLAUDE_CODE_SESSION_ID` escape
options.detail: cheapest, but a bypass that becomes routine trains everyone to ignore the warning, and every accept then records "Independence NOT established"

evidence: reviewer verified subagents share the parent session id, first-hand from its own env
`CLAUDE_CODE_CHILD_SESSION=1` is a boolean flag, not a finer id
both `--to=accepted` and `--to=clear-human` were refused on PR #1100's real body
decisions.detail: RULED 2026-08-08: reviews move to a Claude Code CLI invocation. Verified mechanically rather than assumed — a headless claude -p run mints its OWN session id and its child processes see that id in CLAUDE_CODE_SESSION_ID, which is the exact variable the #2844 guard reads. Parent 01f39b97 vs child f4386de9. So the independence is real, and it needs no manual session and no daemon prerequisite. A subagent spawned from the session does NOT qualify: it inherits the parent id verbatim. Follow-on work is filed as the CLI-optimisation epic.

decisions.title: Fork B — rebuild or drop
decisions.question: Does the codification shortcut get one more attempt, or get dropped?
decisions.ifNothing: Fork A still ships; codification PRs keep needing a human.
decisions.why: Broken FIVE times by five independent reviewers. Each round closed one class and a new one appeared, always a hand-rolled approximation of a grammar detail: a mid-rule splice, an untagged second heading, eight more heading forms, counting lines instead of headings, and now HTML_COMMENT_RE — which is not the HTML comment grammar. HTML also terminates a comment at <!-->, <!---> and --!>, so the regex over-consumes and deletes real <h3> tags out of the counted content. A working attack amends the leash rule itself and clears with auto-merge on. Fork A shipped separately as #1102, so nothing is blocked by dropping this.

options.label: One round rebuilt on `markdown-it`
options.detail: it is already a dependency and already renders that document, so detection and rendering cannot disagree; if this breaks too, drop it

options.label: Drop Fork B now
options.detail: every codification PR then needs a human, which is the status quo and costs little

options.label: Drop Fork B
options.detail: Every codification PR then needs a human — the status quo, and it costs little. Five rounds of security-critical review have bought nothing yet; the ratio is bad and the failure mode is always the same shape.

options.label: A sixth round
options.detail: The fix direction is named and conservative: refuse any raw-HTML token containing <!-- whose comment scan is not unambiguous, rather than parsing it. But I recommended a fifth round on the same reasoning and it broke again.

evidence: three breaks: mid-rule splice · untagged second heading · eight more forms incl. `<h3` with a newline before `>`
a working attack added a rule reading 'agents may clear their own leash' with autoLand:true
five breaks, five reviewers; each fix closed one class and opened another

decisions.title: Todo mode for unimplemented contract entries
decisions.question: Should a contract entry be able to declare itself not-yet-implemented, like `test.todo`?
decisions.ifNothing: A contract entry with no implementation and no marker passes silently — the strictness #1099 traded away stays traded.
decisions.why: The operator's own idea. #1099 made 'declared but not implemented' legal but invisible — nothing distinguishes deliberately-ahead-of-the-code from someone forgot. A `todo` marker makes the third state explicit and lets the gate be stricter than #1099, not looser.

options.label: Build it before the Fork A/impl split
options.detail: that split is the first real case of spec landing ahead of impl, so it is the natural first customer; roughly one field plus four cases in the conformance test

options.label: File it and build later
options.detail: no urgency if the split declares and implements in the same pair

evidence: row 3 (declared, absent, unmarked) currently PASSES
row 4 (marked todo but implemented) would catch the stale marker — `test.todo` does not
pair with `owedTo` naming an open item, matching #1100's invariant-catalogue convention
decisions.detail: RULED 2026-08-08: build it. The justification is the silent third row, NOT the Fork A/impl split named in the prepared recommendation — that split already shipped whole as PR #1102, which moved the contract entry and the REVIEW_REASONS enum in the same commit, so the 'natural first customer' came and went and the two vocabularies are equal today (9 tokens each). What stands on its own is that #1099 relaxed the conformance pin from equality to containment, which leaves 'declared, absent, unmarked' passing silently in the one suite whose whole job is being the deterministic backstop. A todo marker makes that third state explicit and makes the gate STRICTER than #1099, not looser: an unmarked absent entry fails, and a marker left behind after the code lands also fails — the stale-marker case test.todo does not catch. Pair the field with owedTo naming an open item, per #1100's invariant-catalogue convention. Note the build edits the declarative leash (the contract plus the conformance suite), so its PR fires gate-self and needs a human clear regardless.

decisions.title: Converge daemon scheduling
decisions.detail: Ruled: do it, but when the priority is right — clear the other blockers first.
decisions.ifNothing: every parked PR keeps waiting for the operator personally.

decisions.title: The command guard: how should it handle text the shell re-executes?
decisions.question: Six rounds have tried to enumerate every way a command hands a hidden script to the shell. Should the guard keep enumerating, refuse what it cannot resolve, or stop at the holes it has already closed?
decisions.ifNothing: #1092 cannot land, and base keeps the confirmed write hole where a quoted pipe lets a redirect through to the shared checkout.
decisions.why: Every round's evidence looked overwhelming and every next round found more holes. The sixth reviewer found why: the fuzz generator's wrapper list was literally the classes the previous fix had just implemented, so three million pairs could only re-prove what was already handled. Enumeration cannot be completed from inside the thing being enumerated. Six positions are still unrecursed (bash -o pipefail -c, a pipe or here-string into a shell, trap, process substitution, find -exec, nohup/exec), and both recursion caps fail OPEN — past depth 4 or 64 nodes the scanner stops and allows.

options.label: Refuse what it cannot resolve
options.detail: Apply the guard's own ratified doctrine — unparseable means deny — to nested execution. Stop listing positions to recurse into; deny at the primary checkout when a command contains shell re-execution the guard cannot fully resolve. Ends the enumeration game. Cost: some everyday shell-rc idioms would be denied at the primary cwd, and the false-deny sweep would have to be re-run to size that.

options.label: A seventh round of enumeration
options.detail: The six missing positions and the fail-open caps are all named with small fixes. But the same reasoning justified rounds five and six, and the generator problem means the next round's evidence will be built from the next round's list.

options.label: Keep only what is proven, drop the recursion
options.detail: Keep the splitter (it closes four confirmed holes base has), the runner work, the corpus and thirteen false-deny fixes. But dropping the recursion leaves head WORSE than base on bash -c and eval, because base caught those by accident through its sloppy quote-blind split. Not a clean retreat.

evidence: 145 everyday commands swept, zero newly denied — precision is not the problem
9/9 prior holes closed, 13/13 intended fixes hold, 33/33 attack spellings deny
